overview.text: Eyes are sensory organs that begin vision by collecting light; seeing also depends on the brain, which interprets signals sent from each retina. Light first passes through the clear cornea, which helps focus it; the pupil is the opening that admits light, while the iris adjusts its size. Behind it, the clear lens further focuses light onto the retina, a light-sensitive layer lining the back of the eyeball. Retinal photoreceptors convert light into electrical signals, carried along the optic nerve to the brain. The macula supports central vision, and its fovea is where vision is sharpest.

key_facts.text: The cornea is the clear, dome-shaped covering at the front of the eye and helps focus light.
The pupil is an opening in the iris; the iris changes its size to regulate how much light enters.
The lens sits behind the iris and focuses light on the retina, helping the eye focus on near and far objects.
Retinal receptor cells called rods and cones respond to light and send electrical impulses through the optic nerve to the brain.
The macula is a retinal area needed for central vision; its center, the fovea, is where vision is sharpest.
